lessonTitle: Screening, Immunisation and Health Promotion: Screening Criteria, Brief Advice and Motivational Interviewing

blocks.text: A 52-year-old man who smokes twenty a day tells you, politely, that he has no intention of stopping. A lecture on lung cancer would bounce off. Yet five minutes later, when you ask what he enjoys about smoking and what he does not, he says, 'My daughter keeps asking me to stop.' Prevention in primary care depends as much on how you talk as on what you know.

blocks.markdown: **Screening.** Screening is the systematic offer of a test to people with no symptoms, to identify those at increased risk of a disease or its complications so that early treatment improves outcome. It differs from diagnostic testing, which investigates symptomatic patients. Because screening is offered to healthy people, it must do more good than harm. The classic framework is Wilson and Jungner's 1968 criteria, now updated and applied by national bodies such as the UK National Screening Committee.

rows: An important health problem; natural history understood, including development from latent to declared disease; a recognisable early stage
Simple, safe, acceptable to the population, with adequate sensitivity and specificity and a suitable cut-off; agreed follow-up for positives
An accepted, effective treatment for patients with recognised disease, with better outcomes if started early; agreed policy on whom to treat
Facilities for diagnosis and treatment; cost balanced against benefit; case-finding as a continuing process; quality assured
blocks.caption: Check the current UK National Screening Committee criteria and the programmes' current eligibility and intervals before quoting any.

blocks.markdown: **How well does a screening test perform?** Sensitivity is the proportion of people with disease who test positive; specificity is the proportion without disease who test negative. For a rare disease, even a very specific test produces many false positives, so the *positive predictive value* (PPV) can be low. From a two-by-two table:

blocks.caption: $TP$ true positives, $FP$ false positives, $TN$ true negatives, $FN$ false negatives.

blocks.title: Predictive values in a screened population
blocks.prompt: A test with sensitivity 80% and specificity 95% is used to screen 10,000 people. The disease prevalence is 1%. Calculate the number of true positives, false positives, and the PPV.

steps.text: Number with disease: 1% of 10,000 = 100; without disease: 9,900. True positives are 80% of 100.
False positives are the 5% of the 9,900 people without disease who test positive; true negatives are the rest.

Interpretation: about 14% of positives truly have the disease, and 86% are false positives who need explanation, further tests and reassurance. The NPV is 9405/9425, about 99.8%, so a negative result is very reassuring.

blocks.answer: PPV is about 14%: most positives in a low-prevalence population are false positives.

blocks.markdown:
**Harms and biases.** Screening harms include false positives (anxiety and further investigation), false reassurance from false negatives, overdiagnosis (detecting disease that would never have caused harm) and complications of follow-up procedures. *Lead-time bias* makes survival after screen-detected disease appear longer simply because diagnosis is earlier, even if death occurs at the same time; *length-time bias* occurs because screening preferentially detects slow-growing disease. Therefore the outcome that matters is disease-specific mortality, measured in a randomised trial. Informed choice matters: patients need balanced information about benefits and harms, and screening programme details (ages, intervals, tests) change, so check the current programme information.

**Immunisation** is a related population-level preventive measure that works differently: it is offered to everyone eligible to prevent infection rather than to detect disease. Its principles are that vaccines are given according to the national programme (the UKHSA Green Book is the authoritative source; check the current schedule, as it changes), that uptake of high coverage gives herd protection to those who cannot be vaccinated, that contraindications and adverse reactions are checked before each dose, and that consent and clear information are essential. Primary care identifies under-immunised patients, explores the reasons (access, worries, misinformation) with motivational interviewing, and offers catch-up vaccination.

**Health promotion and counselling.** Primary care has repeated, trusted contacts with patients and can make every contact count with *brief advice*. For smoking, very brief advice follows **Ask** (about smoking status), **Advise** (the most effective way to quit is with support and medication) and **Act** (offer or refer to stop-smoking services; pharmacotherapy chosen according to current NICE guidance and the BNF). For alcohol, screen with a validated tool (for example AUDIT-C), calculate weekly units and give brief advice. Current UK Chief Medical Officers' guidance advises that adults should not regularly drink more than 14 units a week, spread over three or more days; check the current guidance. Units of alcohol are calculated from the volume and the strength (percentage alcohol by volume, ABV):

blocks.caption: One UK unit is 10 ml (8 g) of pure alcohol.

blocks.title: Calculating alcohol units
blocks.prompt: A patient drinks a pint (568 ml) of beer at 4.5% ABV. How many units is this?

steps.text: Substitute the volume and strength into the formula.

So a pint contains about 2.6 units. Use this to translate drinks into units and compare weekly intake with the low-risk guidance (check current guidance), and to explain to the patient why a few pints can exceed what they think of as 'a few drinks'.

rows: Ask, Advise, Act; offer behavioural support and pharmacotherapy as per current NICE guidance and BNF; follow up
Screen (for example AUDIT-C); calculate units; brief advice for increasing-risk drinking; refer if dependence is suspected; do not stop abruptly in dependence without medical advice
Individualised, practical advice on a balanced diet and weight, aligned with current national dietary guidance; address cost and cooking skills
Current UK guidance for adults: at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week plus muscle-strengthening; start low and build up (check current guidance)
blocks.caption: Advice should be personalised and followed up; check current UK guidance for the numbers.

blocks.markdown: **Stages of change and motivational interviewing.** The transtheoretical (stages of change) model describes a cycle: *precontemplation* (not considering change), *contemplation* (ambivalent), *preparation* (planning), *action*, *maintenance* and possible *relapse*, from which people re-enter the cycle. Matching the approach to the stage avoids pushing too early. *Motivational interviewing* (MI) is a collaborative, goal-oriented style that strengthens a person's own motivation for change. Its spirit is partnership, acceptance, compassion and evocation. Core skills are summarised as OARS: **O**pen questions, **A**ffirmations, **R**eflective listening and **S**ummaries. Practitioners avoid the *righting reflex* (the urge to fix and persuade), elicit and reinforce *change talk*, explore ambivalence and develop discrepancy between current behaviour and the person's own values.

rows: Build rapport, provide information if invited, ask permission, plant seeds
Explore ambivalence, weigh pros and cons, evoke change talk
Help to set a specific plan and goals, identify support
Reinforce; normalise lapses and learn from them
blocks.caption: The stages are fluid; people move back and forth.

blocks.title: A motivational interviewing exchange
blocks.prompt: A 45-year-old office worker says she wants to be fitter 'someday' but is 'always too busy'. Show how you could respond using MI skills.

steps.text: Open question: 'What would being fitter do for you?' to evoke her own reasons rather than supplying yours.
Reflect: 'It sounds as if being fitter matters to you, but your days are packed.' This conveys understanding and keeps the conversation going.
Affirm and explore: 'You have thought about this a lot. What has helped you fit things in before?' This draws out strengths and past success.
Ask permission to offer information, then summarise and ask an open question about next steps: 'What small step might you be willing to try this week?'; agree a follow-up.

blocks.answer: A collaborative conversation that elicits her own motivation, with a small, self-chosen goal and follow-up.

points: Screening offers a test to asymptomatic people; the Wilson-Jungner criteria assess the condition, test, treatment and programme, and programme details change, so check current information.
PPV depends on prevalence; screening in low-prevalence populations produces many false positives, and biases such as lead-time and overdiagnosis complicate interpretation.
Counsel on smoking (ask, advise, act), alcohol (units = volume x ABV / 1000), diet and activity, using current UK guidance.
Stages of change guide the approach, and motivational interviewing (OARS, evoking change talk, rolling with resistance) strengthens the patient's own motivation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a Wilson-Jungner criterion for a screening programme?

options.text: The condition should be rare and have an unknown natural history
Screening should be offered only to people with symptoms
There should be an accepted, effective treatment for patients with recognised disease
The test must have 100% sensitivity and specificity

questions.correctOptionText: There should be an accepted, effective treatment for patients with recognised disease

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the condition should be an important health problem with a well understood natural history.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: screening is for asymptomatic people.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: an effective treatment is a core criterion.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: no test is perfect; the criterion is an adequate, acceptable test.

questions.explanation: Screening is only worthwhile if early detection allows treatment that improves outcome, so an effective treatment is a core criterion. Perfect tests do not exist, and the other statements contradict the criteria.

questions.stem: A new screening test is introduced and survival from diagnosis lengthens, but the age at death is unchanged. Which bias explains this?

options.text: Lead-time bias
Length-time bias
Recall bias
Selection bias in a randomised trial

distractorRationale.a: Correct: earlier diagnosis lengthens apparent survival without delaying death.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: length-time bias refers to preferential detection of slow-growing disease.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: recall bias concerns inaccurate memory in retrospective studies.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: randomisation protects against selection bias.

questions.explanation: When diagnosis is made earlier, the time from diagnosis to death increases even if death occurs at the same age. This is why disease-specific mortality, not survival after diagnosis, is the correct outcome for evaluating screening.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes very brief advice on smoking?

options.text: Warn the patient about the dangers of smoking and end the consultation
Tell the patient to stop immediately without support
Ask about smoking only if the patient has a cough
Ask about smoking, Advise that the most effective way to quit is with support and medication, Act by offering help

questions.correctOptionText: Ask about smoking, Advise that the most effective way to quit is with support and medication, Act by offering help

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: warnings alone are not effective, and offering help is part of the approach.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: unsupported quitting is less effective.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: smoking status should be asked about routinely.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: this is Ask, Advise, Act.

questions.explanation: Very brief advice is a structured 30-second intervention that identifies smokers, advises on the best way to quit and offers support. Offering help (act) is the step that makes it effective, with pharmacotherapy selected according to current NICE guidance and the BNF.

questions.stem: A man says, 'I know I drink too much, but it is how I relax and I am not sure I could cope without it.' At which stage of change is he, and what is the best approach?

options.text: Maintenance; stop all follow-up
Contemplation; explore the ambivalence and evoke his own reasons for change
Precontemplation; give a stern warning
Action; congratulate him and arrange a review

questions.correctOptionText: Contemplation; explore the ambivalence and evoke his own reasons for change

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: he has not made any change to maintain.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: he recognises the problem but is ambivalent.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: precontemplation means not seeing a problem, and warnings tend to increase resistance.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: he has not yet started changing his behaviour.

questions.explanation: He acknowledges the problem yet remains torn, which characterises contemplation. Motivational interviewing explores ambivalence and evokes the patient's own reasons for change, rather than persuading him.

questions.stem: A patient says, 'I would love to exercise, but I just have no time.' Which response best reflects the spirit of motivational interviewing?

options.text: 'You must exercise or you will have a heart attack.'
'There is nothing I can do if you will not make time.'
'It sounds like finding time is the biggest hurdle. What has helped you fit things in before?'
'Everyone has time if they really want to.'

questions.correctOptionText: 'It sounds like finding time is the biggest hurdle. What has helped you fit things in before?'

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: this uses fear and the righting reflex.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: this reflects, shows empathy and draws out the patient's own strengths.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this confronts and dismisses the barrier.

questions.explanation: A reflective statement shows understanding and keeps the patient talking, and the open question evokes their own solutions. Confrontation and warnings typically provoke resistance.

questions.stem: A patient drinks three 175 ml glasses of wine (12.5% ABV) on each of 4 evenings a week. Using units = volume (ml) x ABV (%) / 1000, calculate her weekly alcohol intake in UK units.
questions.explanation: One 175 ml glass of 12.5% wine is 175 x 12.5 / 1000 = 2.19 units. Three glasses give 6.56 units per evening, and four evenings give 26.25 units per week. This is well above the current low-risk guidance of 14 units a week (check current guidance), so brief advice and follow-up are indicated.

questions.stem: A screening test with sensitivity 90% and specificity 98% is given to 20,000 people in a population where the prevalence of the disease is 0.5%. Calculate the positive predictive value as a percentage, to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: There are 100 people with disease, so there are 90 true positives. Of the 19,900 without disease, 2% (398) test falsely positive. The PPV is 90/(90 + 398) = 90/488 = 0.184, or 18.4%, so most positives are false positives despite the high specificity.

questions.stem: Discuss the potential harms and benefits of a screening programme, and explain why a high-sensitivity test may still be unsuitable for population screening.
markingGuide: Benefits: earlier detection and treatment; reduced disease-specific mortality or morbidity, if the criteria are met
Harms: false positives with anxiety and further investigation; false negatives with false reassurance; overdiagnosis and overtreatment; complications of follow-up procedures
Biases in evaluating screening: lead-time bias, length-time bias, overdiagnosis; need for randomised trial and disease-specific mortality
Predictive values depend on prevalence: low prevalence gives low PPV even with high specificity
Other criteria: an effective treatment, acceptable test, adequate facilities, cost-effectiveness
Informed choice and balanced information; check current programme details
questions.explanation: A strong answer balances benefit and harm and explains why screening differs from diagnostic testing. Recognising the effect of prevalence on PPV and the biases in evaluation shows understanding of why programmes need strict criteria.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man attends for a new patient check and reports that he drinks about 20 units of alcohol a week. Describe how you would assess and counsel him.
markingGuide: Screen using a validated tool such as AUDIT-C; clarify the pattern (binge versus regular) and units per week
Ask about effects on health, work, relationships, mood and symptoms of dependence; assess for withdrawal risk
Explain current UK low-risk drinking guidance (check current guidance) and relate his intake to it
Brief advice with motivational interviewing: elicit his views and readiness to change
Agree goals, offer written information and support, and arrange follow-up
Refer for specialist support if dependence is suspected; advise not to stop suddenly if physically dependent without medical advice
Check liver and other relevant tests as indicated
questions.explanation: The answer should combine a structured assessment (tool, units, dependence) with a patient-centred brief intervention. Hedging on the guideline numbers and following up demonstrate safe practice.

questions.stem: Describe the stages of change and the principles of motivational interviewing, and explain how you would adapt your approach for a patient who is in the precontemplation stage for increasing physical activity.
markingGuide: Stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance, relapse (cyclical)
MI spirit: partnership, acceptance, compassion, evocation; collaborative and patient-led
Skills: OARS (open questions, affirmations, reflective listening, summaries); eliciting change talk
Avoid the righting reflex, confrontation and unsolicited advice; roll with resistance
Precontemplation approach: build rapport, ask permission to discuss, explore values and concerns, offer information neutrally, avoid pushing for action
Leave the door open, review at a later visit, and affirm any step towards change
Relapse is normal and an opportunity to learn
questions.explanation: A good answer names the stages, explains the MI spirit and skills, and then matches the approach to the stage. In precontemplation the goal is to build rapport and plant seeds, not to demand action.
